A choropleth shades each region by a value — emissions, incidence, turnout, income. It is the most
common map in data analysis and the easiest to get *subtly wrong*. The mechanics are simple: join a
table of values to a set of shapes by a common key, then map value to colour. The judgement is in
the rest — what you encode, how you class it, and which palette you choose. This post builds one in
R with [canvasXpress](https://canvasxpress.org) and treats those choices as first-class, not
afterthoughts. The join and the colouring happen inside the render, so every figure here is one
portable spec you can re-run from R, Python or the browser.

## First, the trap: colour encodes a *rate*, not a *count*

A choropleth fills an **area**, and area is a size channel your eye cannot help reading. Shade
countries by a raw count — total cases, total emissions, total sales — and big, populous regions
light up simply because they are big and populous. You have drawn a population map with extra steps.

The fix is almost always to map a **rate or density**: cases per 100k, emissions per capita, sales
per store. Reserve raw counts for a *proportional-symbol* map (a sized bubble at each centroid),
where the size channel carries the count honestly and area is not doing uninvited work. Decide which
question you are answering before you pick the geometry — this one choice prevents most misleading
maps.

## One value per region

A choropleth needs exactly one measurement per shape. In canvasXpress the **columns** are the
regions (they match the map by name) and the **row** is the variable you colour by — here CO₂
emissions per country for 2018. Load a prepared table; swap it for your own (any `country → value`
table works).

```{r}
#| message: false
library(canvasXpress)

y <- read.table(
  "https://www.canvasxpress.org/data/r/cX-CO2-dat.txt",
  header = TRUE, sep = "\t", quote = "", row.names = 1,
  check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

dim(y)              # 1 row (CO2) x N countries
y[, 1:4]
```

The single row is the variable (`CO2`); each column name is a country that must match a shape in the
map. An optional **sample annotation** table (rows = countries) rides along for richer tooltips and
legends — here the continent and ISO code.

```{r}
x <- read.table(
  "https://www.canvasxpress.org/data/r/cX-CO2-smp.txt",
  header = TRUE, sep = "\t", quote = "", row.names = 1,
  check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
head(x)
```

## A first map: one continuous ramp

`graphType = "Map"` with a `topoJSON` of world boundaries draws the shapes; `colorBy = "CO2"` shades
each country on a continuous scale. The countries join to the map by name — no manual merge, no
projection math.

```{r}
canvasXpress(
  data      = y,
  smpAnnot  = x,
  graphType = "Map",
  colorBy   = "CO2",
  topoJSON  = "https://www.canvasxpress.org/data/maps/WORLD.json",
  mapId     = "co2Continuous",
  legendPosition = "left",
  theme = "solarized",
  title = "CO2 emissions per country (2018)",
  width  = 700,
  height = 500
)
```

It renders — but look closely and most of the world is the same pale colour. That is not a bug; it
is the data. Emissions are **heavy-tailed**: a few countries dwarf everyone else, so a linear ramp
spends almost its entire range on the top few and flattens the rest into one indistinguishable band.
A continuous ramp is honest only when the variable is roughly uniform or near-normal.

## Class a skewed scale with natural breaks

When the data is skewed, **class** it: cut the range into a handful of bins and give each bin a
colour. `colorSpectrumBreaksMethod = "jenks"` picks class edges that minimise within-class variance
(Jenks natural breaks) — it finds the gaps the data actually has instead of slicing the range evenly.
Now the middle of the distribution gets colours of its own.

```{r}
canvasXpress(
  data      = y,
  smpAnnot  = x,
  graphType = "Map",
  colorBy   = "CO2",
  topoJSON  = "https://www.canvasxpress.org/data/maps/WORLD.json",
  mapId     = "co2Classed",
  colorSpectrum = list("#fff7ec", "#fdd49e", "#fc8d59", "#d7301f", "#7f0000"),
  colorSpectrumBreaksMethod = "jenks",
  mapColor        = "#e5e7eb",
  mapOutlineColor = "#ffffff",
  legendPosition  = "bottom",
  title    = "CO2 emissions per country (2018), classed by natural breaks",
  subtitle = "Five Jenks classes — a single continuous ramp collapses this to one tone",
  width  = 700,
  height = 500
)
```

Five classes is a good default (three to seven is the usable range — more and readers cannot tell
colours apart in a legend). Swap `"jenks"` for `"quantile"` to put an equal *number of regions* in
each class instead of equal-variance breaks: quantile classing guarantees every colour is used and
is the right choice when you care about ranking regions rather than their absolute spacing.

## Choose the palette on purpose

The palette is not decoration — it is the scale's grammar:

- **Sequential** (light → dark of one hue, as above) for a quantity that only goes up: counts,
  rates, concentrations. Low values pale, high values saturated.
- **Diverging** (two hues meeting at a neutral midpoint) when values are meaningful *above and
  below a reference*: change vs. last year, difference from a target, a signed index. Give
  canvasXpress a three-colour `colorSpectrum` and pin the midpoint with `colorSpectrumZeroValue`:

  ```r
  colorBy = "Change",
  colorSpectrum = list("#2166ac", "#f7f7f7", "#b2182b"),  # blue - neutral - red
  colorSpectrumZeroValue = 0                               # value mapped to the middle colour
  ```

  Never use a diverging palette for a purely positive quantity — the neutral midpoint invents a
  "normal" that the data does not have.

Reach for colour-blind-safe ramps (ColorBrewer, viridis) and keep the *same* scale across small
multiples so maps are comparable. A rainbow ramp is almost always the wrong answer: it has no
perceptual order, so readers cannot tell which end is "more".

## Polish: legend, labels and base styling

A few keys turn a rough draft into something publishable:

- `subtitle` / `source` — caption the units and provenance.
- `legendNumberFormat = list(style = "decimal", decimals = 1, suffix = "%")` — format the legend
  ticks as percentages, currency, etc.
- `mapColor` / `mapOutlineColor` — set the fill for regions with **no data** (grey) and the border
  between shapes, so missing data reads as missing rather than as a value.
- `showMapLabels = TRUE` — draw region names (best on maps with few regions, e.g. a single country's
  provinces; it clutters a 190-country world map).
- `legendInside = TRUE` — float the legend over empty ocean to reclaim width.

## Beyond the world map

- **Other boundaries.** Point `topoJSON` at any shape file — US states, a single country's regions,
  counties, custom districts. The join key is just the shape name.
- **Projection.** `mapProjection = "albers"` (equal-area, good for the US) or `"mercator"`. Equal-area
  projections matter for choropleths: Mercator inflates high latitudes, exaggerating those regions'
  visual weight.
- **Categorical maps.** Point `colorBy` at a categorical column (an election winner, a priority tier)
  for a qualitative choropleth with a discrete legend.
- **Markers.** Add `decorations` to drop labelled points on cities or call out specific regions.

The whole figure — data, boundaries, classing rule and palette — travels together as one spec, so a
reviewer can reproduce it exactly and a colleague can re-render it from Python or JavaScript.
